### BR-0334: P2 - Measure portal clearance instead of destination-center clearance

- [ ] OPEN
- Type: defect
- Confidence: high
- Category: correctness/route-planning
- Found by: R1-CHUNK-0215, R1-CHUNK-0216
- Location: `c01d8fe4686c63d931b1e543a6305bbafaa944a9:android/app/src/main/cpp/shared/secret_area_game_adapter.c:L1453-L1500` in topology clearance construction
- Related: `android/app/src/main/cpp/shared/secret_area_game_adapter.c:L522-L560,L1501-L1509`, `android/app/src/main/cpp/shared/route_snapshot.cpp:L405-L408`, `android/app/src/main/cpp/shared/route_planner.cpp:L328-L338,L884-L895`, `android/tests/test_route_snapshot.cpp:L34-L40,L76-L80,L526-L645`, and `android/ai tool plans/gameplay/kcxf2_automap_scan_and_route_regressions_20260713.md`
- Evidence: The adapter computes one binary clearance value per destination segment by placing a player-sized sphere only at that segment's cached center. If the center does not intersect a wall it returns the full player radius; otherwise it returns one. The continuation then copies that destination scalar to every incoming side, without inspecting the side vertices, portal aperture, source geometry, or a swept path through the connection. Route search treats any copied value at least as large as the navigator radius as proof that the side is traversable. A roomy destination behind a portal narrower than the player therefore passes solely because its center is clear. The inverse heuristic is also topology-dependent: the code acknowledges that skewed but navigable segments can have bad centers, yet relaxes only connected bad-center components smaller than three; three or more such segments retain clearance one and are rejected without testing an off-center route. Snapshot tests inject a clearance number directly and never exercise the engine adapter's derivation.
- Trigger: Load or inspect a custom D1 or D2 level containing two roomy connected segments whose shared portal is narrower than the player sphere while the destination center has full clearance; alternatively connect at least three skewed segments whose centers intersect a wall but which have a valid off-center player path.
- Impact: The shared planner can publish an `ok` route through a passage the player cannot cross, causing Guide-Bot guidance and automap, launcher, headless, JNI, introspection, and automation objectives to stall at the impossible side. The inverse geometry is reported partial or failed even though the player can traverse it, and the arbitrary component-size threshold makes equivalent local geometry change solvability when a third segment is attached.
- Expected: Navigator clearance describes the actual directed connection and a realizable player-sized traversal through its portal; destination-center occupancy alone neither proves nor disproves passage clearance.
- Suggested fix: Compute clearance per side from the portal polygon and adjacent segment geometry, then validate a player-radius swept transition or bounded set of connected occupiable poses across the side. Preserve an explicit unknown state that route search handles conservatively rather than treating zero as unrestricted, and remove the component-count relaxation once valid off-center traversal is represented.
- Validation: Add paired adapter-level geometry fixtures for wide and too-narrow portals between roomy segments, asymmetric portal directions, a clear center with blocked transition, one through four skewed but navigable segments with off-center paths, and genuinely narrow tunnels. Require route reachability to match player-radius physics independent of unrelated component length, with exact snapshot clearance values and matching canonical metadata, live Guide-Bot, automap, headless, JNI, introspection, and automation results.
- Additional location (R1-CHUNK-0216): `c01d8fe4686c63d931b1e543a6305bbafaa944a9:android/app/src/main/cpp/shared/secret_area_game_adapter.c:L1501-L1509` in final side-clearance publication
- Additional evidence (R1-CHUNK-0216): After the component-size heuristic, publication iterates every source side and assigns only `Level_metadata_segment_clearance[child]`. The final route-facing value is therefore provably identical for all portals entering one destination, regardless of each portal's aperture or swept transition geometry.

### BR-0336: P2 - Close route-cache files after short reads

- [ ] OPEN
- Type: defect
- Confidence: high
- Category: resource-lifetime
- Found by: R1-CHUNK-0216
- Location: `c01d8fe4686c63d931b1e543a6305bbafaa944a9:android/app/src/main/cpp/shared/secret_area_game_adapter.c:L1881-L1929` in persistent route-cache loading
- Related: `android/app/src/main/cpp/shared/route_analysis_cache.c:L117-L252`, `android/tests/test_route_analysis_cache.c`, and `android/ai tool plans/gameplay/route_cache_android_audit_20260715.md`
- Evidence: After accepting the reported exact record length and allocating a buffer, the loader combines the complete-read check, `PHYSFS_close(file)`, and decode with `&&`. C evaluates those operands left to right with short-circuiting. If `PHYSFS_readBytes` returns fewer bytes or an error, the close operand is never evaluated. The buffer is freed and the cache is rejected, but the open PhysicsFS file and its underlying descriptor remain owned indefinitely; this branch also increments only `rejections`, not `io_errors`. The length-mismatch and allocation-failure branches close explicitly, so the leak is isolated to a read that becomes short after the length check.
- Trigger: Make an app-private route-cache record report the exact expected length, then truncate or replace it between `PHYSFS_fileLength` and `PHYSFS_readBytes`, inject a filesystem read error, or otherwise return a short read; repeat level loads while the failing record remains addressable.
- Impact: Each failed cache attempt leaks a PhysicsFS handle and native file descriptor until process exit. Repeated mission or level loads under a persistent storage failure or cache mutation can exhaust descriptors and cause unrelated asset, save, music, or cache opens to fail.
- Expected: Every successful `PHYSFS_openRead` is closed exactly once on every read, decode, allocation, and validation outcome, and read failures are counted as I/O errors before falling back to planning.
- Suggested fix: Store the read result, call `PHYSFS_close` unconditionally in a separate statement, and only then combine read, close, and decode results. Classify short or failed reads and close failures as I/O errors while retaining rejection and safe planner fallback behavior.
- Validation: Add an injectable PhysicsFS loader test that reports the exact record length but returns a short read or error, plus a close-failure case. Assert one close per successful open, no increase in process descriptor count over repeated attempts, no decode on incomplete bytes, correct I/O and rejection counters, and successful full-planner fallback.
- Resolution: Pending

The load menu, Save Explorer metadata, and D2 secret companion can then describe different mission generations, and the player loses the prior mission's only saved progress despite the feature promising mission-masked save sets.
- Expected: Every mission identity accepted by the engine maps deterministically to its own collision-resistant save-set namespace, and core saves, last-save pointers, metadata, and D2 companions use the same canonical identity.
- Suggested fix: Define one shared mission-identity encoder used by all save-set artifacts. Preserve the complete canonical basename when practical or combine a readable bounded prefix with a collision-resistant digest; never narrow it before the canonical encoder. ### BR-0339: P1 - Clamp the network overlay within narrow displays

- [ ] OPEN
- Type: defect
- Confidence: high
- Category: correctness

- Location: `c01d8fe4686c63d931b1e543a6305bbafaa944a9:android/app/src/main/java/com/dxxredux/app/multiplayer/NetworkEventsOverlay.kt:L84-L97,L216-L228` in draw-time sizing
- Related: `android/app/src/main/java/com/dxxredux/app/MainActivity.kt:L728-L731,L794-L801,L2230-L2248`, `android/app/src/main/java/com/dxxredux/app/SetupActivity.kt:L4765-L4800`, and `android/app/src/main/AndroidManifest.xml:L51-L57`
- Evidence: Panel width is computed with `(w * 0.32f).coerceIn(160f * density, w * 0.45f)`. Kotlin requires the minimum not exceed the maximum; for every view narrower than `160 / 0.45 = 355.56dp`, this call receives an empty range and throws `IllegalArgumentException` from `onDraw`. The application declares no minimum screen width, exposes and applies a portrait game orientation, and supports configuration changes without recreating the activity. The outer activity automatically calls `show` while a multiplayer launch has not yet reached in-game state and while the host is selecting players, so the crash does not require an obscure direct call or even a manual diagnostic toggle. No test constructs the view or measures it at narrow widths.
- Trigger: Select portrait orientation on a device whose available game width is below 356dp, or place the game in a comparably narrow supported multi-window, then start or host a multiplayer game so the network-events overlay is automatically shown
- Impact: The game process crashes on its first network-overlay draw, preventing multiplayer startup or host player selection on the affected display configuration
- Expected: Diagnostic overlay measurement is total for every nonnegative view size Android can deliver, fits within the available viewport and insets, and never throws because a preferred minimum exceeds the current maximum
- Suggested fix: Derive one nonnegative available content width after padding and insets, choose the preferred width, then clamp it with an ordering-safe `min` against that available width rather than passing a potentially inverted interval to `coerceIn`. Skip drawing at zero size and truncate, wrap, or scroll rows within the bounded rectangle.
- Validation: Add a view or screenshot test across zero width and 240, 320, 355, 356, 360, 600, and large-screen dp widths at several densities, portrait and landscape, cutouts, and multi-window resizing while the overlay is hidden, manually visible, and automatically visible during multiplayer phases. Require no exception and assert the background and every rendered row remain inside the viewport.
- Additional location (R1-CHUNK-0387): `c01d8fe4686c63d931b1e543a6305bbafaa944a9:android/app/src/main/java/com/dxxredux/app/multiplayer/MultiplayerStatsOverlay.kt:L218-L265,L312-L334` in the second network overlay's draw-time sizing and peer rows
- Additional evidence (R1-CHUNK-0387): The manually toggled stats overlay repeats the same inverted-range defect with `(w * 0.3f).coerceIn(180f * density, w * 0.45f)`, so every available width below 400dp throws from `onDraw`. It also computes panel height from up to seven ping rows and seven connection rows plus a fixed 70dp graph without clamping to `h`; at the maximum ordinary roster the panel requires more than 400dp before title-label overflow, so short landscape and multi-window configurations draw diagnostics beyond the viewport even when width is sufficient. This is the same shared overlay-measurement root rather than a separate crash finding.
- Additional validation (R1-CHUNK-0387): Exercise the stats overlay at zero and 240, 320, 399, 400, 480, and 600dp widths, short landscape heights, every roster size from one through eight, direct and relay connection rows, and manual hide and show during live resizing. Require total draw behavior and keep the complete panel, graph, labels, peer rows, and connection rows within available bounds.
- Additional location (R1-CHUNK-0389): `c01d8fe4686c63d931b1e543a6305bbafaa944a9:android/app/src/main/java/com/dxxredux/app/CoopStatsOverlay.kt:L187-L288` in cooperative-overlay draw-time sizing
- Additional evidence (R1-CHUNK-0389): The cooperative overlay adds a third unbounded overlay measurement policy. It derives text size as the lesser of 10dp and 1.3% of raw view width, with no readable minimum, so a 360dp-wide portrait view renders approximately 4.7dp text and narrower multi-window views shrink further. At wider sizes the eight-player plus Guide-Bot panel reaches approximately 278dp high, but drawing never consults `height` or clips, scrolls, or relocates content; supported short landscape and multi-window viewports therefore lose lower teammate rows. This is the same narrow-viewport measurement root, without the inverted-range exception of the other two overlays.
- Additional validation (R1-CHUNK-0389): Add cooperative-overlay view or screenshot cases across phone densities, 240 through 600dp widths, heights below and above 278dp, one through eight connected players, and Guide-Bot present and absent. Require a documented readable text floor and keep every title, score, player, bar, weapon, and owner row visible within the content viewport through bounded scaling, truncation, or scrolling.

### BR-0340: P2 - Stop network overlay polling when its view detaches

- [ ] OPEN
- Type: defect
- Confidence: high
- Category: resource-lifetime
- Found by: R1-CHUNK-0219, R1-CHUNK-0387, R1-CHUNK-0389
- Location: `c01d8fe4686c63d931b1e543a6305bbafaa944a9:android/app/src/main/java/com/dxxredux/app/multiplayer/NetworkEventsOverlay.kt:L23-L60` in self-reposting main-looper polling
- Related: `android/app/src/main/java/com/dxxredux/app/MainActivity.kt:L1771-L1784,L2081-L2292,L2419-L2441`
- Evidence: Once `show` sets `polling`, the runnable captures its overlay, invokes the provider, invalidates, and reposts itself every second. Only explicit `hide` clears the flag and removes that callback; the view has no detach hook. `MainActivity.onStop` removes callbacks from a different `overlayPoller` but does not hide this overlay, and `onDestroy` neither hides it nor clears its provider. If the network overlay is visible when the activity backgrounds or is destroyed, its queued runnable therefore continues forever on the process main looper. The runnable retains the view, whose `Context` retains the destroyed `MainActivity` and its game view graph; repeated sessions can accumulate one retained activity and periodic callback each.
- Trigger: Show the network-events overlay manually or reach an automatically visible multiplayer phase, then background the game, return to the launcher, finish the activity, or recreate it without first executing an explicit overlay-hide branch
- Impact: Background work continues once per second, and destroyed game activities and their large view graphs remain reachable. Repeated game launches can accumulate memory and main-looper work until process death or memory pressure, while detached views receive pointless invalidations.
- Expected: Polling is active only while the view is attached, visible, and owned by a live resumed activity, and every lifecycle exit removes all callbacks and provider references deterministically
- Suggested fix: Start polling from an attached-and-visible lifecycle and unconditionally stop it in `onDetachedFromWindow`; also have `MainActivity.onStop` or `onDestroy` hide or dispose every polling overlay. Clear `stateProvider` on disposal, and use one lifecycle-aware scheduler rather than independent self-reposting handlers where practical.
- Validation: Add lifecycle tests that show the overlay, stop, detach, destroy, recreate, and repeat without an explicit manual hide. Advance the main looper past several intervals and assert no provider calls or callbacks remain, the old activity is garbage-collectable, and resuming or reattaching starts exactly one polling chain.
- Additional location (R1-CHUNK-0387): `c01d8fe4686c63d931b1e543a6305bbafaa944a9:android/app/src/main/java/com/dxxredux/app/multiplayer/MultiplayerStatsOverlay.kt:L24-L33,L102-L129,L144-L215` in self-reposting stats polling and retained providers
- Additional evidence (R1-CHUNK-0387): `MultiplayerStatsOverlay` independently owns the same main-looper handler pattern. Once manually shown, its runnable invokes four activity-installed providers, including two JNI reads, invalidates, and reposts every second. Only explicit `hide` removes it; there is no detach hook, while `MainActivity.onStop` and `onDestroy` do not hide this view or clear its ping, packet, proxy, and connection closures. A visible stats view therefore continues polling while backgrounded and retains the destroyed activity and native access paths just like the already recorded network-events overlay.
- Additional validation (R1-CHUNK-0387): Include both network overlay classes in the lifecycle matrix, with the stats overlay manually visible before stop and destruction. Assert all four provider references are released, JNI and proxy call counts stop immediately, no detached invalidation occurs, and recreation plus repeated toggle produces exactly one polling chain.
- Additional location (R1-CHUNK-0389): `c01d8fe4686c63d931b1e543a6305bbafaa944a9:android/app/src/main/java/com/dxxredux/app/CoopStatsOverlay.kt:L22-L35,L57-L131` and `android/app/src/main/java/com/dxxredux/app/MainActivity.kt:L1508-L1541,L1684-L1725,L1771-L1782,L2419-L2439` in unconditional cooperative polling and activity lifecycle
- Additional evidence (R1-CHUNK-0389): Surface creation starts cooperative polling for every game, including single-player sessions where the view auto-hides, and its runnable invokes three activity-installed JNI provider closures before reposting every second. The view has no detach hook. `MainActivity.onStop` removes callbacks only from its separate 100ms overlay poller, and `onDestroy` neither stops this handler nor clears its providers. Unless the game-started flag later reaches the explicit hide branch, a backgrounded or destroyed activity therefore remains retained by a detached, self-reposting cooperative overlay that continues native reads even while hidden.
- Additional validation (R1-CHUNK-0389): Include the cooperative overlay in lifecycle tests for single-player and cooperative games, hidden and visible states, surface destruction, stop, destroy, recreation, and repeated launches. Assert all three providers and the old activity become unreachable, no JNI call or invalidation occurs after stop or detach, hidden non-cooperative play performs no periodic work, and resume or reattach starts exactly one polling chain.

- Location: `c01d8fe4686c63d931b1e543a6305bbafaa944a9:android/app/src/main/java/com/dxxredux/app/multiplayer/NetworkEventsPanel.kt:L35-L45,L82-L130` in disconnected-state admission and rendering
- Related: `android/app/src/main/java/com/dxxredux/app/multiplayer/MatchmakingService.kt:L274-L308,L846-L904,L911-L930,L1147-L1182`, `android/app/src/main/java/com/dxxredux/app/multiplayer/MatchmakingState.kt:L100-L124`, and `android/app/src/main/java/com/dxxredux/app/multiplayer/NetworkEventsOverlay.kt:L103-L205`
- Evidence: The assigned panel intentionally remains present while `DISCONNECTED` whenever any STUN address, candidate map, connectivity pair, connection record, or relay assignment remains, and it renders those values without a connection or lobby generation. Manual disconnect clears candidates, pairs, connection records, and relay but retains `stunAddrs` and `iceStatus`. More importantly, unexpected WebSocket close and failure clear only the connection record among those diagnostic fields; peer candidates, connectivity pairs, relay assignment, STUN addresses, ICE result, and `stunCompleted` remain from the ended connection. Reauthentication replaces only STUN addresses. If rejoin does not occur, the browser continues to show the old lobby's NAT, peer, address, priority, and relay topology under a disconnected or newly connected badge; if it does occur, new candidate entries are added by peer ID and do not remove departed old IDs until an explicit leave or manual disconnect.
- Trigger: Reach candidate exchange, connectivity checking, or relay assignment in one online lobby, then lose the WebSocket and let reconnect succeed or fail without executing `leaveLobby` or manual `disconnect`
- Impact: The network panel and any snapshot consumer can attribute an old lobby's peers, routes, latency method, relay, and ICE outcome to the current disconnected or replacement connection. Operators diagnose the wrong path, stale peer addresses remain displayed after their session ends, and reconnect state can mix two generations until a later explicit cleanup.
- Expected: Every connection or lobby generation owns its diagnostic fields; close, failure, leave, replacement, and successful reauthentication either clear the ended generation atomically or publish a separately labeled historical record that cannot be mistaken for current state
- Suggested fix: Centralize connection-generation teardown and clear candidate, pair, relay, STUN, ICE, completion-gate, and connection fields together on every terminal path. Assign a generation token to asynchronous STUN and connectivity results and reject late updates from prior jobs. If historical diagnostics are desired, store them separately with terminal status and timestamps.
- Validation: Populate unique diagnostic sentinels, then exercise manual disconnect, clean close, failure, reconnect success, reconnect failure, rejoin to the same lobby, join a different lobby, late STUN completion, and late connectivity completion. Assert current-state fields contain only the active generation, the panel hides or labels history when disconnected, and no old peer ID, address, relay, or ICE result can reappear.
- Resolution: Pending

### BR-0342: P1 - Authenticate LAN lobby control packets and member identities

- [ ] OPEN
- Type: defect
- Confidence: high
- Category: security/protocol-integrity
- Found by: R1-CHUNK-0220, R1-CHUNK-0397
- Location: `c01d8fe4686c63d931b1e543a6305bbafaa944a9:android/app/src/main/java/com/dxxredux/app/lobby/LobbyProtocol.kt:L14-L26,L110-L260,L298-L328` in the unauthenticated JSON-over-UDP lobby message schema and parser
- Related: `android/app/src/main/java/com/dxxredux/app/lobby/LobbyService.kt:L630-L683,L870-L968,L1099-L1155,L1221-L1260`, `android/app/src/main/java/com/dxxredux/app/multiplayer/NetworkConstants.kt:L40-L50`, `android/app/src/main/java/com/dxxredux/app/SetupActivity.kt:L1701-L1740`, and `android/app/src/test/java/com/dxxredux/app/LobbyProtocolStartOptionsTest.kt:L15-L58`
- Evidence: Every LAN lobby datagram is plaintext JSON with a message type and payload fields but no authenticated session, host credential, member credential, sequence, or replay generation. The lobby UUID is broadcast in `ANNOUNCE`, so matching it proves no authority. On the frozen host, `LEAVE` and `READY` select another player solely by payload callsign, and `CHAT` accepts and relays any payload callsign from any sender without requiring membership. On a joiner, `PLAYER_LIST`, `JOIN_REJECT`, and `KICK` do not receive the sender address at all; `JOIN_ACK` accepts any nonempty lobby ID and binds its sender as host without correlating a pending target; and `START` checks at most the public lobby ID, not that the sender is the joined host. The accepted `START` payload becomes a launch event using that sender as `lanHostAddr` and trusts its port, game, mission, mode, difficulty, level, maximum-player count, and options; unsupported modes then silently map to anarchy. The focused test proves ordinary serialization only and has no hostile-sender, identity, replay, or state-transition cases. Later sender/client-ID checks added for `LEAVE` and `READY` do not authenticate the remaining host-control and chat messages.
- Trigger: While another player hosts or joins a discoverable lobby, let any device able to send UDP on the same LAN observe the broadcast lobby ID and transmit forged `LEAVE`, `READY`, `CHAT`, `PLAYER_LIST`, `JOIN_ACK`, `JOIN_REJECT`, `KICK`, or `START` JSON datagrams to port 42400
- Impact: A malicious or compromised LAN peer can impersonate players, change readiness, remove members, falsify the roster, abort or redirect a join, eject joined clients, and force a client to leave setup and launch the native game toward an attacker-selected address and port with attacker-selected mission and rules. Replayed stale control packets can also affect a later state that reuses the same process and lobby identity.
- Expected: Only the established host can alter joiner state or launch and kick a client, only an admitted member can act or chat as that identity, every response is correlated with the exact pending lobby generation, and stale, forged, cross-lobby, or semantically invalid packets are rejected without changing UI or launch state
- Suggested fix: Establish a high-entropy per-lobby host identity and a distinct per-member session credential during a correlated join handshake, then authenticate every state-changing datagram with an AEAD or MAC over its type, lobby/generation ID, sender role, member ID, sequence number, and payload. Bind acknowledgements and rejections to the requested host and nonce, enforce monotonic replay windows, verify exact source and role as an additional check, validate all launch enums and numeric ranges before publication, and rotate credentials whenever hosting or membership restarts.
- Validation: Add a two-client hostile-peer matrix for every message type covering wrong source, wrong member, copied callsign, public lobby ID, unsolicited and mismatched acknowledgements, spoofed rejection and player list, kick for another target, forged and replayed start, reordered and duplicate sequence numbers, stale packets after leave/rejoin and host restart, and malformed launch fields. Assert no unauthorized state, liveness timestamp, chat attribution, retry cancellation, membership, readiness, diagnostic, or launch event changes; then verify ordinary join, reconnect, mid-game join, chat, ready, kick, start, packet loss, and app resume still work.
- Additional location (R1-CHUNK-0397): `c01d8fe4686c63d931b1e543a6305bbafaa944a9:android/app/src/main/java/com/dxxredux/app/multiplayer/MultiplayerResumePrefs.kt:L58-L71` and `android/app/src/main/java/com/dxxredux/app/multiplayer/LanDiscoveryTab.kt:L370-L402` in saved-host matching and direct resume
- Additional evidence (R1-CHUNK-0397): A client resume can retain a stable `hostClientId`, but the matcher deliberately falls back to public callsign, game, mode, and mission whenever a responding announcement omits its host ID. `tryJoinLobbyByIp` accepts that predicate while querying the saved address. An unauthenticated responder can therefore strip the one stable comparison field and satisfy the fallback metadata, so the resume path does not strengthen BR-0342's spoofable announcement and join boundary.
- Additional validation (R1-CHUNK-0397): Save a LAN host ID, then answer the direct resume query from the expected and reassigned addresses with missing, wrong, copied, and correct IDs plus matching public metadata. Require a record that has stable identity to fail closed on missing or mismatched authenticated identity and never join or launch from fallback display fields.
- Resolution: Pending

- Evidence: The branch adds allocator runtime metadata to paired save formats. The setter copies the values into live globals and immediately loops from zero through the attacker-controlled `Highest_object_index`, indexing `Objects[i]`. The D1-in-D2 translator validates only the two scalar ranges before copying the equally unvalidated free list into the same paired setter.

A malformed local save or transferred checkpoint can therefore crash the game, corrupt allocator and object state, or silently reuse a live slot; cooperative restore can distribute the same unsafe image to peers.

- Suggested fix: Parse into temporary storage and validate `num_objects`, `highest_object_index`, every relevant free-list entry, uniqueness, the used/free partition, and correspondence with `Objects[].type`; validate the signature and homer scalar domains as well. Make the setter return failure without mutation, propagate that failure through paired restore and translation entry points, and combine it with staged restore so invalid images cannot leave partial live state.

- Related: `d1/main/state.c:L2140-L2202`, `d1/main/object.c:L866-L886,L1042-L1068`, `d1/main/render.c:L1436-L1450`, `d1/main/ai.c:L1519-L1526`, `android/app/src/main/cpp/shared/input_demo_start_shared.c:L400-L445,L589-L590`, and `android/app/src/main/cpp/shared/input_demo_replay.cpp:L240-L257`
- Evidence: The exact-order checkpoint helper first clears every segment head, but then publishes each candidate `Segments[segnum].objects` head incrementally while validating saved `prev` and `next` topology. On a later duplicate root, invalid index, reciprocity mismatch, cycle, disconnected object, or similar failure, it returns false without removing already published heads. Its caller treats false as a compatibility signal: after resetting only the object allocator, it loops through every live object and calls `obj_link` without clearing segment heads or object links again. `obj_link` prevents only the new object's index from already being the immediate head; it does not prevent a stale head from pointing through the rebuilt list back to itself. With three live objects in one segment and stale head 2, fallback insertion of objects 0, 1, and 2 leaves head 2 and next links `2,0,1`, so traversal repeats `2->1->0->2`. Render and AI consumers follow the segment list until `-1` without a cycle bound. The checkpoint checksum authenticates bytes but imposes no topology semantics, so a crafted checkpoint can carry its own matching checksum and reach this path through ordinary input-demo startup.
- Trigger: Start a D1 input demo whose checkpoint has a valid base image, object count, and checksum but malformed saved object-link topology that makes exact-order restoration fail after at least one segment head has been published
- Impact: Restore can report success with a cyclic segment object list. The next render, AI, collision, or other unbounded traversal can loop forever on the game thread, repeatedly process objects, corrupt state further, and force process termination. A small crafted local demo therefore provides a deterministic denial of service.
- Expected: Invalid checkpoint topology is rejected without mutating live segment or object links, and no successful compatibility fallback can reuse partially restored graph state. Every successful restore leaves each live object reachable exactly once from one acyclic segment list.
- Suggested fix: Stage candidate segment heads and link metadata separately, validate the complete graph before publishing any global link, and return an explicit malformed-checkpoint failure instead of conflating it with legacy compatibility. If a compatibility fallback remains, first clear every segment head and every live object's `next` and `prev`, then rebuild from a known-empty graph and validate exact coverage and acyclicity before restore succeeds.
- Validation: Add malformed checkpoint cases for duplicate roots, invalid indices, broken reciprocity, cycles, disconnected objects, repeated objects, and failure after one or more candidate heads have been processed, plus valid empty, single-object, multi-segment, and non-index-ordered lists. Require no link mutation on validation failure, bounded completion under a short render and AI watchdog, exactly-once live-object coverage after fallback, and no cycle or invalid access under ASan/UBSan.
- Additional location (R1-CHUNK-0315): `c01d8fe4686c63d931b1e543a6305bbafaa944a9:d2/main/state.c:L1510-L1593,L2857-L2883` in current-save object-link validation and fallback, with `d2/main/object.c:L1254-L1278` in `obj_link`
- Additional evidence (R1-CHUNK-0315): D2 independently adds the same unsafe state transition to every current save restore. `state_restore_segment_object_links` clears the segment heads, publishes a head for each serialized root, and can then return false on a later duplicate root, invalid reciprocal link, cycle, or incomplete coverage. `state_restore_all_sub` immediately calls `state_relink_objects_by_index`, which resets each object only as it reaches that slot and never clears the partially published segment heads. If a stale higher-numbered head remains while lower-numbered objects are inserted first, `obj_link` links those objects through the stale head; when that head's own slot is later reset and inserted at the front, its previous chain can point back to it. The resulting cycle is accepted as a successful ordinary, cooperative, rewind, or checkpoint restore and reaches the same unbounded engine traversals. Live D2 retains this behavior.
- Additional trigger (R1-CHUNK-0315): Restore a D2 state with at least three live objects in one segment and serialized links that publish a higher-numbered root before failing a later topology check, through a local save, launcher resume, cooperative transfer, rewind image, or input-demo checkpoint
- Additional validation (R1-CHUNK-0315): Run the malformed topology corpus through all D2 restore entry points as well as D1 checkpoint startup. Assert validation failure leaves no segment head or object link mutated; if compatibility fallback is intentionally retained, start it only from a fully cleared graph and prove every live object is reachable exactly once with bounded render, AI, collision, and object-list diagnostics.

- Evidence: The branch replaces terminal object-sync failure with a three-attempt retry counter. On a count or player verification failure, the client clears `Network_rejoined`, resets only local counters, and returns while remaining in `NETSTAT_WAITING`. The host, however, has already processed the same stream's end marker by calling `net_udp_send_rejoin_sync`, which marks the joining player's host-side slot `CONNECT_PLAYING` before sending the sync datagram. That sync immediately follows the end marker and the client-side `net_udp_read_sync_packet` has no requirement that the object stream succeeded: with `Network_rejoined` now false it takes the new-level branch, relinks player objects, and unconditionally sets `NETSTAT_PLAYING`. Thus the ordinary queued sync can admit the client with the incomplete object array that verification just rejected. If that sync is lost or deliberately ignored, polling resends `UPID_REQUEST`, but host welcome-slot selection returns `ANDROID_NET_UDP_WELCOME_SLOT_ALREADY_CONNECTED` for the already-playing slot and sends no objects, so the retry counter can never reach a second actual stream. The branch's explicit `net_udp_request_resync_from_host` has the same mismatch: it changes only the client's local connected state, while the host still sees a playing slot and rejects every repeated request. The sole maintained caller uses this path when a cooperative restore image is missing.
- Trigger: Lose enough D1 or D2 rejoin object datagrams to make object-count or required-player verification fail, or let a cooperative client receive a restore command whose save ID is missing or mismatched and invoke the explicit host resync request
- Impact: A lossy rejoin can report success and enter gameplay with missing robots, players, powerups, hostages, or control-center objects, causing immediate divergent simulation, invalid object references, later crashes, or corrupted cooperative state. If the trailing sync is absent, or on the explicit missing-save path, the client instead remains in a waiting state that sends requests forever while the host refuses to restart the stream. The advertised three retries never occur.
- Expected: Failed object verification cannot transition to play, each admitted retry starts a fresh complete object stream on both peers, and an explicit in-game resync has a host-recognized state transition with bounded success or terminal failure. Live object state is published only after one verified stream and matching sync generation complete.
- Suggested fix: Replace the implicit `UPID_REQUEST` reuse with an explicit generation-bound resync handshake. Keep the host slot in a syncing state until the client acknowledges successful object verification, tag the object stream and sync with the same generation, ignore an early or stale sync after failure, and make the host restart a complete stream for a valid resync request even when the prior slot was playing. Stage or reset partial client objects between attempts, reset retry state per session, and terminate cleanly after the documented number of actual failed streams.
- Validation: In paired D1 and D2, drop, duplicate, and reorder each object datagram, the end marker, and the following sync; force count mismatch, missing-player verification, a lost first sync, and a missing cooperative restore save. Assert that no client enters play before complete object coverage is verified, each retry produces a distinct full stream, stale syncs are ignored, success occurs within the configured bound when a later stream is complete, terminal failure exits waiting state, and host and client object sets, owners, links, inventory, and connection states match exactly.

- Evidence: Full game-info and sync packets have one sequential wire layout and negotiate compatibility through `MULTI_PROTO_VERSION`. The branch inserts the new host-migration `Multi_master_playernum` byte immediately before the player and netgame tokens, but both its writer and reader are wrapped in `#ifdef __ANDROID__`. The protocol-version constants and request checks are not platform-specific. Consequently an Android sender emits one more byte than a same-source desktop receiver consumes, so the desktop reader treats the master byte plus the first three token bytes as its token. In the reverse direction, Android consumes the first token byte as the master slot and reads the four-byte token one byte late, past the desktop datagram's logical end. A sync token therefore mismatches and is rejected; a full game-info token is corrupted before the late length check rejects or leaves unusable state. Lite discovery can still work because that separate packet omits this tail, making same-version games visible before the full join fails. D1 and D2 repeat the same platform-conditional offset.
- Trigger: Use frozen builds from the same source and protocol version to join a D1 or D2 UDP game between Android and Windows, Linux, or macOS, with either platform hosting
- Impact: Cross-platform peers advertise protocol compatibility and can discover one another but cannot complete full game-info, initial sync, rejoin, or host-migration exchange. Multiplayer between the Android port and maintained desktop builds is therefore broken by construction, while the failure is presented as a token or join problem rather than an explicit incompatible protocol.
- Expected: A negotiated UDP protocol version has exactly one byte layout on every supported platform. Platform-specific behavior may interpret a field differently but cannot insert or remove bytes from the shared packet without a separately negotiated capability or version.
- Suggested fix: Serialize and consume the master-slot field unconditionally in paired D1 and D2 builds, provide a platform-neutral default and validation for builds without Android host migration, and keep the protocol-version bump tied to that layout. Alternatively define a length-delimited, capability-negotiated extension whose presence is explicit before token parsing; do not infer it from the local compile target.
- Validation: Add byte-exact D1 and D2 game-info and sync golden vectors produced and consumed by Android, Windows, Linux, and macOS configurations. Exercise every host/join direction, ordinary and observer joins, rejoin, direct and proxy routes, and host migration; require identical field offsets and lengths for one protocol version, successful token validation, explicit version rejection for old layouts, and a complete cross-platform gameplay sync.
- Resolution: Pending

- Evidence: The paired current-format readers publish three classes of serialized references without proving the writer invariants their consumers require. A record with a valid effect, `EF_ONE_SHOT`, a frame at rollover, negative `time_left`, and an invalid segment or side reaches `do_special_effects` on the next tick; its only topology checks are `Assert` calls, after which release builds directly index `Segments[segnum].sides[sidenum]`. Second, the morph reader checks the object number, signature, render type, and available slot, but then trusts every model-dependent array and scalar. Third, the stuck-object reader clamps only the aggregate count and copies all records without checking object or wall indices. D1's per-frame cleanup scans a slot regardless of the count and indexes `Objects[objnum]` for any `wallnum != -1`; D2's count-gated cleanup indexes both `Walls[wallnum]` and `Objects[objnum]`. Thus short values such as 32767 reach native arrays within at most `MAX_STUCK_OBJECTS` ticks. - Impact: A crafted local or transferred state can drive release builds into out-of-bounds native reads or writes during ordinary effect animation, morph rendering, or stuck-object maintenance, causing deterministic process crashes, adjacent-state corruption, sanitizer termination, or platform-dependent behavior. For morphs, validate the object's model, model and submodel counts, active-state domain, each start point and morphing-point span against `MAX_VECS` and the model data, aggregate active counts, saved control and movement types, and physics fields. ### BR-0361: P2 - Sequence seeded RNG state before recording it

- [ ] OPEN
- Type: defect
- Confidence: high
- Category: correctness/determinism-diagnostics
- Found by: R1-CHUNK-0252
- Location: `c01d8fe4686c63d931b1e543a6305bbafaa944a9:d1/maths/rand.c:L148-L165` in `d_srand_annotated`, with paired `d2/maths/rand.c:L179-L196`
- Related: `android/app/src/main/cpp/shared/input_demo_rng_trace.c:L192-L240,L349-L381`, `android/tests/compare_input_demo_rng_trace.ps1:L37-L54,L96-L140,L256-L290`, `android/tests/test_rng_seed_resume.c:L11-L132`, `android/tests/test_input_demo_recorder.cpp:L312-L319`, `d1/main/collide.c:L1268-L1283`, `d1/main/laser.c:L1470-L1485`, and paired D2 seed callers
- Evidence: After seeding the selected stream, the paired C wrappers invoke `input_demo_rng_trace_record_srand` with `d_rand_get_stream_state(stream, &state_after)` as one argument and `state_after` as the next argument. C does not specify which function argument is evaluated first, so a compiler may read the adjacent `state_after` value while it still holds its initialized zero and only afterward execute the getter that replaces it with the new LCG state. The trace can therefore serialize zero instead of the seeded state even while setting `has_state_after` true. The JSONL writer emits that value as canonical `state_after`, and the maintained comparer skips FX events but compares every SIM reseed line byte-for-byte except source line and sequence numbers. Ordinary active-game paths reseed SIM during deterministic multiplayer egg drops and smart-child creation, so recording and optional replay tracing reach the wrapper after trace startup. A trace captured by one compiler or optimization can falsely mismatch replay on another, while a consistently stale value makes the seed transition internally contradictory and hides the actual post-seed state needed to diagnose the next RNG divergence. The focused RNG test exercises state and sequence restoration without starting a trace, and the recorder test checks only that an `srand` record exists, not its state fields.
- Trigger: Record or trace-replay D1 or D2 on the internal LCG backend through any simulation reseed, such as a multiplayer player drop or smart weapon, using a compiler or optimization that evaluates the `state_after` value before the state-getter argument; compare that sidecar with a trace produced under a different evaluation choice or inspect the reseed transition
- Impact: The deterministic replay diagnostic can report a false first mismatch across supported builds or record an impossible reseed transition whose declared post-state does not equal its seed. Developers can pursue the wrong divergence point or fail a valid cross-build replay comparison, undermining the trace specifically where it is intended to establish the new RNG sequence boundary. Gameplay RNG state itself is still seeded correctly.
- Expected: Every trace record is assembled from fully evaluated, sequenced local values; a successful LCG reseed record always reports `has_state_after=true` and `state_after=seed`, independently of compiler, architecture, optimization, or argument evaluation order.
- Suggested fix: Evaluate `has_state_after = d_rand_get_stream_state(stream, &state_after)` in its own full expression before calling the trace recorder, as the paired random-draw wrapper already does, and pass only side-effect-free locals to the recorder. Keep D1 and D2 identical and consider a small trace-event builder that prevents future producer calls from mixing mutation and observation in argument lists.
- Validation: Extend the paired RNG test to start a trace, perform SIM and FX reseeds with zero, one, high-bit, and maximum seeds, write and parse the JSONL, and assert exact stream, call count, before-state presence, `state_after`, and seed fields. Compile and run at debug and optimized settings with the maintained MSVC and Android Clang toolchains, compare the resulting SIM traces byte-for-byte, and add a source or compiler-warning check for argument-order-dependent state capture. Require ordinary rand records and `NO_WATCOM_RAND` no-state behavior to remain unchanged.
- Resolution: Pending

### BR-0364: P1 - Lock the MVE queue while trimming startup audio

- [ ] OPEN
- Type: defect
- Confidence: high
- Category: concurrency/memory-safety
- Found by: R1-CHUNK-0265
- Location: `c01d8fe4686c63d931b1e543a6305bbafaa944a9:d2/libmve/mveplay.c:L277-L315,L384-L432,L551-L577` in queue accounting, the SDL_mixer postmix callback, callback registration, and Android startup trimming
- Related: `d2/libmve/mveplay.c:L593-L681`, `d2/arch/sdl/digi_mixer.c:L87-L113`, `d2/main/movie.c:L104-L160,L382-L493`, and `android/ai tool plans/mixed batch, umbrella/plan_four_bugs_study.md`
- Evidence: `create_audiobuf_handler` installs `mve_audio_callback` as SDL_mixer's postmix callback before any movie audio starts. That callback has no `mve_audio_playing` gate: whenever the ring is nonempty, it copies from the head buffer, updates `mve_audio_curbuf_curpos`, frees consumed buffers, clears their slots, and advances `mve_audio_bufhead`. The new Android branch in `play_audio_handler` calls `mve_audio_queue_bytes` and `mve_audio_discard_lead_bytes` while `mve_audio_playing` is still false. Those helpers independently traverse the same head state, advance the same cursor, free the same buffers, and advance the same head, but take no SDL audio lock. The producer path explicitly locks only after `mve_audio_playing` becomes true, so no synchronization protects this new startup operation. If the active SDL_mixer device invokes postmix during the trim, both consumers can select the same head: one can free it while the other copies it or both can free it, and an unsynchronized queue-length scan can also observe mixed head, tail, length, and cursor state. Pausing mixer channel zero does not disable the device's postmix callback.
- Trigger: On Android with SDL_mixer enabled, start a D2 MVE after enough audio chunks have been queued to exceed the new 150 ms target while the mixer callback overlaps `MVE_OPCODE_STARTSTOPAUDIO` queue measurement or trimming
- Impact: Movie startup can intermittently read freed audio, double-free a movie buffer, corrupt the ring or allocator, skip arbitrary queued data, or crash during an intro, title, or ending movie. Timing depends on the audio callback, so the failure can evade ordinary functional playback checks and vary by device.
- Expected: Exactly one synchronized consumer owns queue-head advancement and buffer reclamation, and every non-callback operation that reads or mutates callback-owned ring state excludes the active SDL audio callback even before the movie is marked playing.
- Suggested fix: Hold `SDL_LockAudio` across startup queue measurement and the entire discard operation, then unlock before starting playback. Prefer also gating the postmix callback with an explicit movie-audio-active state and unregistering it during teardown, with all queue publication, trimming, draining, and reset transitions following one documented lock and ownership protocol.
- Validation: Add a synthetic MVE fixture that queues more than 150 ms before `STARTSTOPAUDIO`, and instrument barriers so the postmix callback pauses immediately before copying and freeing the head while the engine attempts queue measurement and discard. Under ASan and TSan, repeat startup, abort, end, and restart paths across mono and stereo, compressed and raw audio, and multiple source and mixer rates; require no concurrent access, invalid free, corrupted indices, or unexpected discarded duration. Run the same stress case on Android devices with varied callback sizes and require stable startup audio and movie completion.
- Resolution: Pending

### BR-0366: P1 - Bound D1 frame replacement writes before appending them

- [ ] OPEN

- Category: input-validation/memory-safety

- Evidence: The branch expands `D1_BITMAPS_SIZE` from 300,000 bytes to a fixed 5 MiB, promotes the allocation cursor to the global-lifetime `Bitmap_replacement_next`, broadens the initial wall replacement set, and adds `load_d1_bitmap_frame`. Every new effect and powerup frame and as many as 210 imported robot object bitmaps are appended after the initial wall data. `bitmap_read_d1` obtains `zsize` either from a file-controlled RLE integer or from file-controlled bitmap dimensions, assigns `data = *next_bitmap`, advances the cursor by `zsize`, and calls `PHYSFS_read` into that address without checking the allocation's remaining bytes, the seek result, the file extent, or exact read completion. RLE remapping can then change the encoded size and advances the cursor again. Both callers assert the cursor is below `D1_BITMAPS_SIZE` only after decoding and remapping have already written through the unchecked pointer, so even an enabled assertion detects the condition after heap corruption; the loader nevertheless publishes the bitmap slot and reports success. The maintained design plan explicitly leaves replacement of the fixed `D1_BITMAPS_SIZE` estimate as future work.
- Trigger: Install, register, or expose a corrupt or modified `descent.pig` accepted by D1-in-D2, make an in-range effect, powerup-vclip, or robot bitmap reference select a header whose RLE size or dimensions exceed the bytes remaining after wall replacements, and start a D1 level through the D2 executable. A structurally valid replacement aggregate larger than the fixed estimate exercises the same boundary without a malformed individual size.
- Impact: D1-in-D2 level startup writes past the 5 MiB heap allocation before it can diagnose exhaustion, corrupting neighboring allocator or game state. The result can be an immediate native crash, a later invalid free or rendering crash, or silent bitmap and object-state corruption; a configured bad D1 asset makes the failure repeat on each launch.
- Expected: Every bitmap header, data span, decoded span, and aggregate append is validated before mutation; replacement storage grows from checked exact requirements or enforces a documented aggregate ceiling, and any failure leaves the cursor, bitmap slot, replacement generation, and prior live assets unchanged.
- Suggested fix: Replace the raw global pointer with an owned replacement arena carrying base, used, and capacity. Validate PIG table arithmetic and header/data offsets with checked-width operations, reject nonpositive or oversized RLE lengths and invalid dimensions, require successful seeks and exact reads, and reserve enough space before exposing a destination pointer. Decode and remap into temporary owned storage so the final size is known, grow the arena with checked arithmetic or reject it, then commit the bitmap and cursor atomically. Deduplicate repeated source bitmap indices where practical and propagate a typed load failure that can abort D1-in-D2 activation cleanly.
- Validation: Add synthetic registered-PC, OEM, and Mac PIG fixtures whose selected raw and RLE frames leave exactly zero, one byte, and one frame of capacity; sizes at `-1`, zero, remaining bytes, remaining plus one, `INT_MAX`, and truncated payloads; RLE remaps that shrink, preserve, and grow data; and valid effect, vclip, wall, and all 210 robot references with repeated and unique indices. Require deterministic pre-write rejection, bounded allocation, unchanged prior bitmap pointers and cursor on failure, no leak or partial publication, actionable asset identity and reason, and unchanged rendering for every supported retail D1 PIG.

- Evidence: Ordinary missile creation assigns `Missile_viewer` only when no camera target exists, and the renderer clears that pointer when `PlayerCfg.MissileViewEnabled` is false or the selected object ends. The branch moves robot waking out of the renderer into an unconditional end-of-game-frame call, but `get_missile_camera_viewer` never checks `MissileViewEnabled`. When the pointer is absent or invalid it scans every live object, selects the oldest qualifying local missile, and writes it back to `Missile_viewer`; the wake pass then performs visibility queries and sets zero-awareness robots to weapon-collision awareness. This recreates the pointer every frame after the disabled renderer clears it. It also replaces an ended selected missile with another older in-flight missile, which the next render accepts as the camera target even though the creation path deliberately did not replace an occupied target. The determinism plan required moving the same camera-wake behavior to simulation, not broadening camera admission or lifetime.

Restore clears every `Guided_missile` entry, scans `Objects` in ascending index order, and overwrites the player's pointer for every qualifying guided missile, so the highest object slot wins. Release relinquishes control without deleting the old missile, and later firing assigns control to a newly allocated missile. The free-list allocator reuses recently freed slots, so a writer-valid session can have an older released guided missile in a higher slot and the newer controlled missile in a lower reused slot. Restore then transfers control, steering, and the guided camera to the older missile. No creation timestamp or signature comparison repairs this ambiguity, and no save test covers multiple live guided missiles or slot reuse.
- Trigger: Disable the persisted Missile view option and fire a concussion, homing, smart, mega, flash, mercury, or earthshaker missile within sight of an unaware robot; enable Missile view, fire two qualifying missiles while the first owns the camera, and let the first end while the second remains in flight; or release an in-flight guided missile, free a lower object slot, launch and control a second guided missile into that reused slot, then save and restore while both remain live
- Impact: With missile view disabled, unseen missile positions still wake nearby robots and change their awareness and subsequent AI behavior. With it enabled, a camera whose selected missile ended can jump to another older missile rather than showing the established static or empty transition. Restore can likewise transfer the player's steering and guided view from the missile controlled at save time to an older released missile. The supposedly presentation-only preference, camera target lifetime, and restored control target therefore change gameplay and visible behavior after the determinism and save-state refactors.
- Expected: The simulation wake pass and save/restore pipeline preserve the exact missile identity selected by the owning creation, release, and control transitions, without synthesizing a replacement from object-array order.
- Suggested fix: Separate camera-state ownership from robot waking. Maintain the selected missile identity when the creation or guided-camera path admits it, clear it on the same lifetime transitions independent of rendering, gate ordinary missile-camera waking on `PlayerCfg.MissileViewEnabled`, and make the wake helper consume that state without scanning for or assigning fallback missiles. Serialize the controlled guided missile's object number and signature, validate them against the fully restored live weapon and parent identity, and restore exactly that selection or none; do not infer ownership from the object census.
- Validation: Add D2 gameplay and current-save tests with Missile view enabled and disabled, one and two overlapping qualifying missiles, guided small- and big-window modes, control release, a newer guided missile in a lower reused slot than an older released missile, target deletion, signature mismatch, slot reuse, local restore, rewind, cooperative transfer, replay, and headless execution. Assert exact `Missile_viewer` and `Guided_missile` identity and lifetime plus robot awareness and steering before and after each transition; require no wake for disabled ordinary missile view, no fallback jump after the selected missile ends, exact controlled-missile restoration, and identical simulation outcomes between rendered and headless runs for the same preference state.

### BR-0369: P1 - Give automap failure cleanup one owner

- [ ] OPEN
- Type: defect
- Confidence: high
- Category: error-handling/memory-safety
- Found by: R1-CHUNK-0279
- Location: `c01d8fe4686c63d931b1e543a6305bbafaa944a9:d2/main/automap.c:L1098-L1119,L1241-L1252` in automap close handling and Android background-PCX failure
- Related: `d2/arch/sdl/window.c:L63-L102` and `d2/include/u_mem.h:L52`
- Evidence: The new Android failure arm first frees `am->edges` and `am->drawingListBright`, then calls `window_close(automap_wind)`, then calls `d_free(am)` again. `window_close` is synchronous: it dispatches `EVENT_WINDOW_CLOSE` before returning. The automap handler receives the same `am` as window data, frees its bitmap and child arrays, and calls `d_free(am)`. Although `d_free` nulls the particular lvalue passed to it, nulling the handler's local `am` does not update the caller's local pointer. Control therefore returns to the failure arm with a dangling non-null `am`, and its final `d_free(am)` passes the already freed allocation to `free` a second time.
- Trigger: On Android, enter the D2 automap when `MAP_BACKGROUND_FILENAME` is missing, corrupt, truncated, unreadable, or otherwise rejected by `pcx_read_bitmap`
- Impact: The intended graceful asset-error path executes an invalid double free and can abort in allocator checks, corrupt the native heap, or crash later, so a damaged or incomplete game-data installation still terminates the game process instead of returning safely with a warning.
- Expected: Exactly one owner releases the automap state and its children on every initialization failure, and closing its window cannot leave a second cleanup path holding a stale pointer.
- Suggested fix: Let the registered `EVENT_WINDOW_CLOSE` handler own the initialized window data: after the warning, call `window_close(automap_wind)` and return without manually freeing the child arrays or `am`. If partial initialization requires distinct behavior, centralize cleanup in one idempotent helper and make window/data ownership explicit before invoking callbacks.
- Validation: Add an injectable PCX-read failure test for missing, truncated, malformed, and allocation-failing backgrounds on Android. Open and close the automap repeatedly under ASan or HWASan and allocator diagnostics; require one window close, one release of every automap allocation, restoration of the game window and input/time state, no stale active pointer, no invalid free or leak, and successful automap entry after restoring a valid background.
- Resolution: Pending

- Related: `d2/2d/rle.c:L39-L56,L371-L438`, `d2/arch/ogl/ogl.c:L3535-L3549`, `d2/main/texmerge.c:L224-L227,L283-L286`, `d2/main/collide.c:L669`, `d2/main/fvi.c:L890,L1374`, and `d2/main/gameseq.c:L893-L908`
- Evidence: For an RLE custom bitmap, the loader accepts any declared `data_size >= 4` whose aggregate extent fits the file, allocates exactly that many bytes, and publishes the file bytes with attacker-controlled positive width and height. It does not require the `4 + height` byte row-size table, prove that row sizes stay within the allocation, require row terminators, or bound each decoded row to `width` pixels. Software expansion immediately forms `bm_data + 4 + bm_h`, reads every row-size byte, and calls `gr_rle_decode`, which reads until a terminator and writes run counts without source or destination bounds. OpenGL upload repeats the same operations. Thus a bitmap with positive height and declared size 4 passes the loader but makes the first consumer dereference beyond the four-byte allocation; a longer malformed row can also overrun the width-by-height destination.
- Trigger: Mount a PhysFS-visible D1 mission `.pg1`, `.dtx`, or `.pog` containing an in-range replacement with positive dimensions, `BM_FLAG_RLE`, and either a four-byte declared payload, a truncated row table or row, a missing terminator, or runs that decode beyond the declared width, then load or render the affected texture
- Impact: Mission-controlled bytes cause out-of-bounds reads and writes during texture merge, collision or FVI transparency sampling, software expansion, or OpenGL upload. The game can crash or corrupt heap memory while loading or entering a modded mission, so the branch is unsafe to distribute with this asset path enabled.
- Expected: No custom bitmap becomes visible until its complete encoded structure is proven to fit the source allocation and every row is proven to decode to the supported destination width without overrun.
- Suggested fix: Parse and validate the RLE payload into a temporary exact-size bitmap before mutating `GameBitmaps`: require a complete row table, checked row-span sums within `data_size`, an in-span terminator for each row, and exactly the permitted decoded width with checked run totals. Reject unsupported flag variants and dimensions, and commit the replacement only after every structural and allocation check succeeds. Prefer a shared bounded RLE decoder so later consumers cannot reintroduce unbounded reads or writes.
- Validation: Add malformed custom-asset tests for payload sizes 0 through `4 + height`, exact and one-byte-short row tables, zero and oversized row lengths, missing and early terminators, truncated run pairs, runs decoding to width minus one, exactly width, and width plus one, maximum dimensions, offset boundaries, and multi-entry files where a later entry fails. Under ASan and UBSan, exercise OpenGL upload, texmerge, collision, and FVI sampling; require rejection without slot mutation or leaked saved-original state and successful load and teardown for valid raw and RLE controls.

### BR-0390: P1 - Validate restored scheduler ticks before array indexing

- [ ] OPEN
- Type: defect
- Confidence: high
- Category: security/memory-safety
- Found by: R1-CHUNK-0314
- Location: `c01d8fe4686c63d931b1e543a6305bbafaa944a9:d2/main/state.c:L871-L873,L935` in runtime-state parsing and publication, `d2/main/game.c:L415-L427` in `calc_d_tick`, and `d2/main/wall.c:L1474-L1488` in `remove_obsolete_stuck_objects`
- Related: paired `d1/main/state.c:L652-L654,L709`, `d1/main/game.c:L393-L405`, and `d1/main/wall.c:L1001-L1011`; `d2/main/d1_save_translate.c:L1049-L1118`; `d2/main/state.c:L667-L692`; `android/app/src/main/cpp/jni_resume_save.cpp:L378-L399,L444-L497,L611-L656`; BR-0353 and BR-0360
- Evidence: The branch adds the internal 50 ms scheduler's count, step, and timer to paired runtime save footers. Each reader accepts three arbitrary signed 32-bit values and `game_set_d_tick_state` copies them directly into live globals. On the next frame, `calc_d_tick` resets only the step. If the restored timer remains below its threshold, a negative `d_tick_count` survives unchanged. Both games then compute `d_tick_count % MAX_STUCK_OBJECTS` and use the signed result directly as a `Stuck_objects` index. In C, a negative dividend produces a negative remainder: a saved count of -1 and a below-threshold timer therefore select `Stuck_objects[-1]`. D1 performs that access unconditionally; D2 performs it whenever the same footer restores a nonzero bounded stuck-object count. Independently, a timer of `INT_MAX` overflows at `d_tick_timer += FrameTime`, and an `INT_MAX` count with a threshold-ready timer overflows at `d_tick_count++` before the later million-tick reset. The writer produces only a count in `0..1000000`, a boolean step, and a small nonnegative sub-tick timer. Local saves, cooperative transfers, rewind images, input-demo checkpoints, and D1-in-D2 translation all reach the unchecked setter, and live source retains it.
- Trigger: Load or resume a current D1 save or checkpoint whose runtime footer sets `d_tick_count=-1` and `d_tick_timer=INT_MIN`; for D2, use the same scheduler values and a valid nonzero stuck-object aggregate. Advance one ordinary game frame. Alternatively use `INT_MAX` for the timer or a threshold-ready count to reach immediate signed overflow in `calc_d_tick`.
- Impact: A small malformed local or transferred state can drive the first post-restore frame into a native out-of-bounds read and possible write adjacent to `Stuck_objects`, or into signed-overflow undefined behavior. The game can crash after reporting a successful restore, corrupt nearby wall or object state, or behave differently across compilers; cooperative restore can distribute the same image to peers.
- Expected: Serialized scheduler state is accepted only when it lies in the exact writer-reachable domain, is internally consistent, and cannot produce a negative or overflowing tick before any consumer indexes with it.
- Suggested fix: Parse scheduler fields into temporary storage with the rest of the runtime footer. Require `count` in `0..1000000`, `step` in `0..1`, and a nonnegative timer bounded consistently with the engine's admitted frame-time policy, use checked arithmetic for the next tick, and reject the complete restore before mutation when any field is invalid. As defense in depth, normalize the modulo index to a nonnegative value or use an unsigned bounded scheduler generation before indexing, but do not let that substitute for save validation.
- Validation: Add paired D1/D2 ordinary-save, cooperative-transfer, rewind, input-demo, and D1-in-D2 fixtures with count and timer values at `INT_MIN`, -1, 0, exact writer maxima, maximum plus one, and `INT_MAX`, combined with zero and nonzero valid stuck-object sets. Advance at least one frame under ASan and UBSan and require rejection before global mutation, no negative index or overflow, and unchanged pre-restore state. Retain valid round trips at count wrap, just below and at the 50 ms threshold, and across checkpoint replay.
- Resolution: Pending

This is a release-blocking failure of the server's credential and identity trust boundary even though exploitation additionally requires certificate misissuance and network position.
- Expected: The locked production graph contains a maintained Rustls-WebPKI release with all published verification fixes, and standard validation rejects any vulnerable or unmaintained runtime dependency before deployment.
- Suggested fix: Update the compatible Rustls, Tokio-Rustls, Reqwest, and resolved Rustls-WebPKI pins together so the lock resolves at least `rustls-webpki 0.103.13`, remove or replace the separately unmaintained `rustls-pemfile` dependency with `rustls-pki-types::pem::PemObject`, and add a noninteractive locked Cargo Audit or OSV Scanner step to `rust_lint.sh` and deployment validation. - Validation: Run the advisory gate against the old lock and require failure for the named verifier records, then require a clean result from the updated lock. ### BR-0404: P2 - Generate a deterministically invalid proof-of-work fixture

- [ ] OPEN
- Type: defect
- Confidence: high
- Category: test-gap/determinism
- Found by: R1-CHUNK-0358
- Location: `c01d8fe4686c63d931b1e543a6305bbafaa944a9:server/tests/integration.rs:L1873-L1922` in `test_keypair_auth_bad_pow`
- Related: `server/tests/integration.rs:L35-L59,L1663-L1677`, `server/src/pow.rs:L5-L20`, and `server/src/ws_handler.rs:L539-L599`
- Evidence: The test sends the fixed solution `"0000000000000000"` and comments that it is "almost certainly wrong", then unconditionally expects `AUTH_FAIL`. The test server uses difficulty 8, so any nonce whose SHA-256 challenge concatenation begins with one zero byte is valid with probability 1/256. The challenge is freshly random on every run, making the fixture nondeterministic by construction. Repeated execution reproduced the exact failure twice: one bounded loop first failed after 501 attempts, and a second output-retaining loop failed after 19 attempts when the server correctly returned `AUTH_OK` for the supposedly bad nonce.
- Trigger: Run the maintained integration suite when the random challenge happens to make the fixed all-zero nonce satisfy the configured eight-bit proof threshold
- Impact: A correct server intermittently fails its required integration suite, producing false regression signals and encouraging blind retries. At one execution per suite the expected failure rate is about 0.39 percent, and repeated local, CI, upgrade, and release validation compounds it.
- Expected: Negative proof-of-work coverage constructs a solution that is verified to be below the active challenge's threshold before sending it, so rejection is deterministic for every random challenge and configured test difficulty.
- Suggested fix: After receiving the challenge and difficulty, search for a candidate whose `verify_pow` result is false and assert that precondition locally before sending it. Alternatively derive a valid solution and mutate or select another nonce in a loop until verification is false; do not rely on a guessed constant.
- Validation: Run the focused negative test thousands of times across difficulties 0, 1, 8, and the supported upper boundary. Require deterministic setup or an explicit no-invalid-solution policy at difficulty 0, rejection for every constructed invalid proof, acceptance for paired valid proofs, and no random failure in repeated full-suite runs.

### BR-0421: P2 - Block ordinary launches while the game process is still occupied

- [ ] OPEN
- Type: defect
- Confidence: high
- Category: concurrency/lifecycle
- Found by: R1-CHUNK-0381
- Location: `c01d8fe4686c63d931b1e543a6305bbafaa944a9:android/app/src/main/java/com/dxxredux/app/GameActivityState.kt:L16-L35,L48-L69` in marker publication and live-process discovery
- Related: `android/app/src/main/java/com/dxxredux/app/MainActivity.kt:L678-L711,L1761-L1795,L2419-L2439`, `android/app/src/main/java/com/dxxredux/app/SetupActivity.kt:L135-L152,L1770-L1816,L2006-L2038,L2102-L2133`, `android/app/src/main/java/com/dxxredux/app/SetupAutomationApi.kt:L764-L766`, `android/ai tool plans/testing/report_20260612_220011_autosave_missing_pilot_timeout.md:L23-L36`, and BR-0078
- Evidence: MainActivity writes `game_activity_state.json` on creation and resume, but catches every write or replace exception without reporting failure; destruction deletes the marker before the separate `:game` process is guaranteed gone. `readReturnableGameActivityState` also returns null for an absent, transiently unreadable, malformed, or stale-PID marker even when `readRunningGameProcessPid` independently proves that the package's `:game` process still exists. SetupActivity sets its ordinary `gameRunningFlag` only from the returnable marker on creation and resume, labels the primary action Launch rather than Return, and its normal click and command paths check only that flag and marker before calling `startActivity`. In contrast, automation explicitly checks the raw process PID, waits five seconds, kills a lingering owner, and waits again before launching; setup introspection also reports the raw process as running. The checked-in timeout report documents the exact divergent state—no returnable marker while `:game` still existed—and says a new transient launch was routed into that stale process. The normal user path retains the same admission gap. MainActivity uses only `singleTop`, so a prior instance that is not top or an occupied process with a torn-down Activity can receive a new instance and another surface/native-start request; BR-0078 establishes that duplicate engine admission in one process can corrupt global native state and crash.
- Trigger: Let marker publication fail because app-private storage is full or an I/O/replace operation fails, make the marker unreadable, or return to Setup during the interval after MainActivity clears the marker but before `:game` exits; while the process still appears in `runningAppProcesses`, press the ordinary Launch button or send the ordinary `launch` setup command
- Impact: The launcher presents a fresh launch even though the game process cannot safely host one. It can create a second MainActivity and race a second native engine against the existing or terminating owner, reproducing the known SDL/OpenGL/PhysicsFS global-state crash; alternatively the new Activity can be rejected, misrouted, or left without the game the UI claimed to launch. A still-returnable game can also lose its Return to Game affordance solely because its advisory file failed.
- Expected: A live `:game` process is an occupied admission state even when no trustworthy returnable-activity marker exists. Ordinary UI and command launches wait for confirmed process exit or recover the exact existing activity; marker failure is visible and cannot be interpreted as permission to start another engine.
- Suggested fix: Model `none`, `returnable activity`, and `occupied/unreturnable process` explicitly from one lifecycle owner. Combine marker and raw-process checks for every UI, command, resume, demo, and multiplayer launch gate; show Return only for a validated activity, and disable Launch with a finishing/recovery state while any unmatched process remains. Reuse a bounded, lifecycle-aware version of the automation wait without killing a user game silently. Publish the marker through `AtomicFile` or an equivalent checked durable helper, return write/clear failures, and reconcile ownership using a per-activity generation rather than PID alone. BR-0078's native atomic owner must remain the final defense.
- Validation: Instrument marker create, write, flush, rename, read, parse, and delete failures; storage-full conditions; process death and PID replacement; Activity destruction before process exit; HOME/recents/launcher transitions; and simultaneous ordinary, command, resume, demo, and multiplayer launch attempts. At every boundary require exactly one native owner, no enabled Launch while an unmatched `:game` PID exists, correct Return only for the matching live activity generation, bounded recovery after exit, explicit diagnostics, and no duplicate Activity, native startup, crash, hang, or wrong-game routing under repeated race stress.
- Resolution: Pending

### BR-0422: P2 - Release retained gyro axes whenever gyro production stops

- [ ] OPEN
- Type: defect
- Confidence: high
- Category: correctness/input-lifecycle
- Found by: R1-CHUNK-0382
- Location: `c01d8fe4686c63d931b1e543a6305bbafaa944a9:android/app/src/main/java/com/dxxredux/app/GyroInputManager.kt:L57-L80,L92-L165` in configuration, lifecycle, conditional activation, and axis dispatch
- Related: `android/app/src/main/java/com/dxxredux/app/MainActivity.kt:L870-L886,L1761-L1796,L2751-L2787`, `android/app/src/main/java/com/dxxredux/app/InputMixer.kt:L21-L26,L47-L59,L81-L127`, `android/app/src/main/java/com/dxxredux/app/TouchOverlayView.kt:L3176-L3199`, and `android/app/src/test/java/com/dxxredux/app/InputMixerTest.kt:L7-L24,L27-L43`
- Evidence: Every active sensor sample sends each configured value to `InputMixer.setAxis(axis, "gyro", value)`, which durably retains that source value until the same source sends another value, `clearSources("gyro")` is called, or all input is released. No gyro path calls that clearing API. When `TOUCH_STICK` activation ends, the overlay zeros the touch axes and sets `rightStickActive` false, but the next gyro event returns after zeroing only diagnostics; it emits no zero axes. `ADS_ONLY` inactivity behaves identically. Disabling through the runtime toggle calls `setConfig` and `pause`, and Activity stop unregisters the listener, but neither path clears the gyro mixer source. Changing axis bindings similarly starts emitting on new axes without removing the old source entries. Therefore the last nonzero gyro contribution remains in the additive mixer after its producer is inactive or gone; the focused mixer test confirms retained gyro values survive removal of another source, while no test exercises producer deactivation or remapping.
- Trigger: Enable gyro, tilt far enough to emit a nonzero value, then release the shared right stick in `TOUCH_STICK` mode, turn gyro off with Gyro On/Off, disable it through a reloaded layout, or remap a nonzero gyro axis while the game remains active
- Impact: The ship can continue turning, pitching, banking, or sliding at the last gyro value with no active gyro gesture or sensor producer. Ordinary stick input is added on top and may only mask or saturate the stale contribution; recovery requires reactivating and centering gyro, stopping the Activity so `releaseAll` runs, or restarting.
- Expected: Every transition that makes a gyro axis inactive, disabled, paused, removed, or remapped atomically removes all prior gyro-source values and dispatches the newly mixed values, normally zero unless another source remains.
- Suggested fix: Give `GyroInputManager` an explicit source-release callback or make MainActivity own gyro producer generations. Track the previously mapped axis set and call `inputMixer.clearSources("gyro")` when conditional activation changes from active to inactive, before unregistering, before disabling, and before applying mappings that remove or change an axis. Prefer dispatching each complete gyro vector atomically so disabled and omitted axes are cleared in the same transaction. Make cleanup idempotent and do not clear touch or controller sources.
- Validation: Seed nonzero values on one, two, and three gyro axes, combine them with touch and controller sources, then exercise stick release, ADS/toggle release, runtime on/off, config disable, each axis remap or disable, recalibration, Activity stop/resume, and sensor loss. Require exactly one updated mixed vector, no retained `"gyro"` entry, preservation of other-source values, zero native motion when no other source remains, and no transient wrong-axis pulse under rapid repeated transitions.
- Resolution: Pending

- Evidence: The editor offers every `GyroActivation` value and labels the third option `ads only`. For that mode, every sensor event defines activity solely as `toggledOn`. The property is initialized false, and a complete frozen-repository search finds no assignment or method that can change it. The configurable `Meta: Gyro On/Off` control appears to be the documented dedicated toggle, but MainActivity intercepts it to flip `GyroRuntimeState.activeInGame`, then disables and unregisters or reenables the entire manager; it never writes `toggledOn`. - Impact: One of the three advertised and documented activation modes is completely nonfunctional.
