- Evidence: Host start runs from a Compose main-thread callback while `handleJoin` runs in the IO receive coroutine. `startGame` reads the roster into `players`, builds `START`, and only afterward sets the volatile `gameStarted` flag; there is no mutex, actor, generation, or atomic StateFlow transformation spanning those operations. A join that passes the old flag before the assignment can be appended and acknowledged after `startGame` captured its recipients, so that admitted player never receives `START`. A join observed after the assignment takes the separate "mid-game" branch, which sends only `JOIN_ACK` and returns without emitting or sending a start launch. This is reachable without precise packet scheduling: announcements are sent only every three seconds, so after the host presses Start, every client still rendering the last `status="lobby"` announcement follows the ordinary `joinLobby` path until the next broadcast. Its acknowledgement sets `_joinedLobby`, cancels retries, and leaves it on the lobby screen; later in-game announcements only update discovery state and never convert that joined client to `emitInGameJoinLaunch`. The original audit required rejecting post-start joins, but the frozen implementation instead acknowledges them without completing either lobby or native late-join protocol. `startGame` also lacks an already-started/generation guard, so a rapid second UI activation can create another independent three-send coroutine and launch event.
- Trigger: Press Join from a waiting-status discovery card during the three-second interval after the host presses Start; alternatively barrier a `JOIN` after its `gameStarted` check but before roster append while the UI thread captures the start roster
- Impact: The host enters the native game while the accepted client remains indefinitely in launcher setup, despite receiving a successful join acknowledgement and continued host announcements. Host and client disagree about membership and launch generation; duplicate start activation can additionally resend stale control state and publish a second launch event. The advertised in-progress join feature therefore fails at the ordinary waiting-to-running boundary.
- Expected: Waiting membership admission and the transition to one game generation are serialized. Every client is either included in that generation's authoritative start recipients, rejected without becoming joined, or given a complete correlated in-game launch path; start itself is idempotent for the generation.
- Suggested fix: Own hosted lobby state in one serialized actor or mutex and transition atomically from Waiting to Starting with an immutable member snapshot and generation ID before sending. Route every subsequent join by that state: reject it so discovery can refresh, or return one complete authenticated in-game launch response carrying the current endpoint and settings. Correlate acknowledgements and starts as required by BR-0342, make repeated start calls return the existing generation rather than launching new jobs, and cancel that generation on stop.
- Validation: Build a two-client test with barriers before and after the join state check, roster append, start-state transition, recipient snapshot, each send, and launch publication. Combine stale waiting announcements, fresh in-game announcements, packet loss and retries, exact-boundary joins, duplicate taps, stop/rehost, background/resume, and later genuine in-game joins. Require each client to receive exactly one rejection or one complete launch for the correct generation, no acknowledged client to remain in setup, no admitted member to be omitted from start, and no stale or duplicate job to relaunch either side.

- Evidence: The manifest runs `MainActivity` in `:game` while `SetupActivity` remains in the default process, and the game explicitly opens Setup without terminating itself. On return, `onResume` says it will reread preferences changed in Setup, obtains `dxx_prefs` with `MODE_PRIVATE`, and uses that process-local object for touch-overlay enablement, skip-intro, cooperative indicator, headlight, music, graphics debug, alpha effects, dynamic-light color, and the graphics-settings generation. Its deprecated reload flag is documented as unreliable and directs apps to explicit cross-process data management. Apply and acknowledge one generation on the engine thread, retain the latest generation for reconnect, and make startup fetch the complete snapshot. Do not use deprecated `MODE_MULTI_PROCESS` as a repair; coordinate the config-file snapshot with BR-0199 so native application cannot rewrite values before all keys are captured.
- Validation: Add multiprocess instrumentation that warms `dxx_prefs` in `:game`, mutates every live preference and graphics key from default-process Setup, resumes repeatedly, and asserts the exact new generation and native snapshot without restarting either process. Cover rapid successive edits, combined edits, `apply` and durable-write failure, process death and reconnect on each side, stale and duplicate generation delivery, D1/D2 config selection, and simultaneous renderer activity; require ordered exactly-once-or-idempotent application and no rollback under BR-0199's corrected atomic snapshot path.
- Additional location (R1-CHUNK-0439): `c01d8fe4686c63d931b1e543a6305bbafaa944a9:android/app/src/main/java/com/dxxredux/app/MusicControlPanel.kt:L736-L773` and `android/app/src/main/java/com/dxxredux/app/MusicPickerPage.kt:L118-L167` in game-to-launcher source-preference publication and consumption

The Music Picker and launch policy read those same keys in the default process. If Setup remains alive with an already loaded preferences object, returning from a game can therefore display and launch with its stale source policy even though the in-game panel and native config accepted the new source. No IPC generation, fresh provider read, or acknowledgement carries the reverse update.

- Evidence: Both native menus request `showKeyboard` as soon as their front selected item becomes an input field. A controller down event can itself move to or activate that field, so the Java callback can run before the same physical key or hat returns to neutral. `showKeyboard` immediately sets `keyboardActive`, focuses the hidden editor, and assigns `hatXState = 0` and `hatYState = 0` without dispatching the releases those states represent. Hiding the keyboard again only zeros the same hat fields and changes focus; it does not release any of those gameplay states. This happens while the Activity remains foreground and therefore does not reach `onStop`'s partial release path from BR-0202. Existing tests verify helper behavior only when matching down and up reach the same owner and never open a paired native text field between them.

- Impact: The game can retain a pressed direct joystick button, mapped action, D-pad direction, or nonzero flight axis after the user has released the control. Native menu holds can activate or reorder unexpectedly, later gameplay can move or fire without input, and the native cutscene release gate can remain armed because `g_joy_buttons_down` never clears. The edge tracker can also suppress the first fresh post-keyboard press until an otherwise unmatched release repairs its bookkeeping.
- Expected: Moving controller ownership from gameplay/native menus to the IME atomically publishes releases or neutral values for every active gameplay button, HAT direction, and axis before new events are rerouted; no physical edge is split between owners and fresh input works immediately after keyboard dismissal.
- Suggested fix: Centralize controller ownership in one lifecycle-aware router. Before setting `keyboardActive`, snapshot and release every tracked direct joystick button, dispatch releases for active HAT directions, clear the `"ctrl"` source from `InputMixer`, and only then reset the edge tracker and transfer new events to the IME. Use an ownership generation so a physical release from the pre-IME generation is consumed without targeting either new owner, and make hide, focus loss, Activity stop, and device removal idempotently neutralize the same state. Coordinate direct SDL release failures with BR-0245 rather than assuming release publication succeeded.
- Validation: Add paired D1/D2 Activity/native instrumentation for every input-field type. Open each field while holding every face and shoulder button, Select, D-pad key, HAT direction, stick axis, trigger, mixer-mapped action, and meta action; release before, during, and after UI-thread keyboard activation, then hide by commit, Back, B, focus change, and native closure. ### BR-0497: P1 - Authenticate and bound dynamic host-proxy peer admission

- [ ] OPEN
- Type: defect

- Category: security/resource-exhaustion

- Location: `c01d8fe4686c63d931b1e543a6305bbafaa944a9:android/app/src/main/java/com/dxxredux/app/multiplayer/LocalhostProxy.kt:L63-L73,L149-L186,L194-L259` in unknown-sender host-mode admission

- Evidence: Host-migration setup binds a shared socket on the advertised host proxy port with `allowDynamicPeers=true`. For every datagram not matching an existing direct address or relay slot, `sharedReceiveLoop` checks only that the process-wide list contains fewer than eight proxies. It then allocates the next loopback port, inserts the sender address permanently, starts forwarding and keepalive coroutines, and immediately delivers the triggering bytes to the engine. There is no pending-player identity, signed request, lobby or game generation, endpoint allowlist, challenge, packet-type gate, per-source budget, admission rate, timeout, or peer removal. The eight-entry cap therefore limits total damage but is itself the denial target: eight datagrams from distinct source ports consume every slot for the proxy lifetime, and later legitimate senders are only logged as unmatched. Native request authentication can reject forged game semantics, including the live remediation archived under BR-0225, but it happens after the proxy has irreversibly spent its local port, list entry, map entry, socket, and coroutines.
- Trigger: After a migrated host advertises or exposes port 42425, send one UDP datagram from each of eight distinct source address-and-port pairs before the legitimate reconnecting peers send their first packets
- Impact: A same-LAN sender, reachable Internet sender after a mapping, or malicious participant can prevent every legitimate reconnect or late peer from reaching the migrated engine until the proxy is torn down and recreated. Each admitted sender also gains a stable loopback route for arbitrary packet attempts and consumes a bound socket plus long-lived coroutines, so native packet rejection does not restore capacity.
- Expected: Dynamic proxy state is allocated only for a player and game generation authorized by matchmaking or a cryptographically proven native join, with bounded pending work, fair capacity, expiration, and deterministic release; unauthenticated traffic spends no persistent peer resources and never reaches the engine as an admitted route.
- Suggested fix: Replace first-packet admission with a generation-bound pending-peer registry populated by authenticated signaling. Require a high-entropy per-player route credential or challenge before allocating the loopback proxy, validate the source against that pending record, rate-limit failed proofs before object creation, and expire and remove both pending and established routes on timeout, rejection, leave, kick, generation change, and shutdown. If native authentication must remain authoritative, add a bounded stateless or single-socket pre-auth path and promote a route only after native approval rather than reserving one of eight permanent entries first.
- Validation: Exercise zero through eight legitimate peers plus hostile packets from one and many source ports before, during, and after migration; copied addresses, callsigns, client IDs, credentials, and stale generations; NAT rebinding; reordered and replayed proofs; capacity and timeout boundaries; leave, kick, failed join, stop, and rehost. Assert unauthenticated traffic allocates no local port, list or map entry, job, keepalive, or engine delivery; every authorized peer receives one stable route; expired capacity is reclaimed; and floods cannot delay or exclude a legitimate pending peer.

- Evidence: `peerProxies` and `jobs` are ordinary mutable array lists with no mutex, actor, thread confinement, immutable snapshot, or stopped generation. They are appended from signaling callers in `addPeer` and from the shared IO receive coroutine in `addDynamicPeer`; `getStats` iterates the peer list; and UI, WebSocket close or failure, replacement, and host-migration callers invoke `shutdown`, which iterates both lists, closes resources, cancels jobs, and clears the collections. An addition can therefore invalidate a fail-fast iterator and abort shutdown, or occur after the corresponding close or cancellation loop and before `clear`. In the latter schedule, the new proxy's shared real socket is closed, but its independently bound `localSocket` was never visited; its local-to-real coroutine can remain blocked in `receive`, the job handle and proxy are cleared, and a later proxy generation cannot bind that port. `shutdown` publishes no stopped flag, so a receive already in progress or a late server message can still call an add path while teardown runs. Existing diagnostics catches iteration exceptions and displays an empty snapshot, but teardown callers do not consistently contain them and no focused concurrency test exists.
- Trigger: Flood a host-mode proxy with new source endpoints, or deliver a late-join approval, while the user disconnects, the WebSocket fails or closes, a replacement proxy is created, or runtime diagnostics iterates proxy stats
- Impact: Teardown can throw before closing the shared socket and clearing service state, or can lose a newly created proxy and coroutine after clearing their only handles. The launcher can retain bound loopback ports, blocked IO jobs, stale forwarding state, and unusable capacity across disconnect or proxy replacement; a later game may silently fail peer binding or receive traffic through the wrong generation. Stats can transiently disappear, and an uncaught shutdown exception can interrupt the surrounding disconnect or failure transition.
- Expected: One serialized owner admits, removes, snapshots, and tears down peers and jobs for an explicit proxy generation. Once stopping begins, no new work can publish; shutdown idempotently closes and joins every resource created by that generation before exposing completion.
- Suggested fix: Confine all proxy commands to one actor or guard state with a mutex and explicit `RUNNING`, `STOPPING`, and `STOPPED` generations. Recheck generation after every socket bind and before publication, close attempt-owned sockets when admission loses a race, take immutable diagnostic snapshots through the owner, reject late commands, and make shutdown suspend until the receive loop and every peer child has completed. Prefer structured child ownership over a separately mutated job list.
- Validation: Use barriers at receive completion, socket bind, list and map insertion, job launch, every shutdown iteration, socket close, cancellation, clearing, and diagnostics snapshot. Race static and dynamic add, late approval, repeated shutdown, disconnect, WebSocket failure, proxy replacement, and hostile floods. Assert no concurrent-modification exception, no post-stop publication, every opened socket closes exactly once, every child completes, maps and snapshots belong to one generation, ports rebind immediately, and stale packets or commands cannot reach a replacement proxy.

Support LAN servers through a scoped trust configuration that validates the entered hostname and a pinned certificate or public key, with explicit fingerprint enrollment and rotation if needed. Resolve once under a deadline, classify the complete result set according to an explicit LAN policy, and pass that bound result or a verified DNS policy into the authenticated TLS connection from BR-0499. Publish typed resolving, invalid, timeout, and connection errors to state rather than collapsing lookup exceptions to public classification.

- Evidence: The migration receiver calls `MatchmakingService.createProxy(listenPort = 42425)` before locating or reading either game's `host_migration.json`. `createProxy` first shuts down the current client proxy, then binds a new host socket and publishes the replacement. If neither file exists, the receiver returns with that replacement already active; if file read, JSON parsing, or field conversion fails, the catch only logs and likewise retains the host proxy without starting a host lobby. Socket construction and bind occur before the receiver's `try`, so a bind exception escapes `onReceive` after the prior proxy has already been shut down and leaves the service field referring to that stopped proxy. The migration file is deleted best-effort only after lobby publication, with no transaction or rollback tying the file, proxy generation, and lobby generation together. Existing BR-0005 covers who can trigger the exported receiver, BR-0497 covers unauthenticated peers after a host proxy exists, and BR-0498 covers concurrent proxy collection mutation; none preserves the previous working generation when the migration attempt itself is invalid or fails.
- Trigger: Deliver a legitimate migration notification while the migration file is missing, partial, malformed, unreadable, or contains a non-integer numeric field; alternatively make port 42425 unavailable when the receiver begins replacing a working client proxy
- Impact: The launcher can silently tear down the route used by the running peer without publishing a valid replacement lobby, preventing reconnect, migration recovery, or continued proxy traffic. A bind failure can also escape the main-thread broadcast callback and crash or recreate the launcher. Because no prior proxy or migration generation is retained for rollback, retry behavior depends on residual file and socket state rather than an explicit recoverable outcome.
- Expected: A host-migration attempt validates one complete, current migration record and proves all replacement resources can be acquired before it retires the active proxy; failure preserves the complete prior generation and reports a retryable result.
- Suggested fix: Read a single game-qualified migration record into a typed, fully validated model first, including bounded game, mission, mode, difficulty, level, and player-count fields plus an explicit migration generation. Build and bind a candidate proxy without mutating the service's current owner, then serialize one commit that swaps proxy and lobby state only after every prerequisite succeeds. On any read, parse, validation, bind, or lobby-publication failure, close attempt-owned resources, keep or restore the prior proxy and record, and surface a typed diagnostic. Delete the migration record only after successful commit and verify or durably retry that cleanup.
- Validation: Starting from a functioning client proxy and lobby, inject missing and dual files, stale generations, partial and malformed JSON, every absent or wrong-typed field, read denial, occupied port, socket construction and bind failures, lobby start failures, deletion failure, duplicate delivery, and process death at each boundary for D1 and D2. Assert every failure leaves exactly the complete prior generation reachable with no launcher crash or leaked socket, one valid attempt atomically publishes exactly one host proxy and lobby, duplicate or stale records cannot replace it, and a retry deterministically completes or reports the retained blocker.

- Evidence: The `LaunchedEffect` is keyed by `refreshTrigger`. It asks `findStaleFiles` for every present game filename with no entry or a changed length, then hashes each one. `computeSha256` catches every file-open or read exception and returns null, so a still-present unreadable file receives no manifest entry and remains stale. After the loop, SetupScreen calls `onRefresh` whenever the original `staleFiles` list was nonempty, even if no digest succeeded; that increments `refreshTrigger` and immediately restarts this same effect. A persistent I/O fault, readable-directory mismatch, or mounted removable file that remains visible but cannot be read therefore creates an unbounded no-delay retry loop. Each iteration resets Compose hashing state, dispatches another IO attempt, logs the same failure and warning, and schedules another recomposition. The earlier hashing-loop cleanup fixed duplicate case variants but did not add failure admission, retry state, or a terminal outcome. Focused tests cover duplicate manifest and disk entries only and never execute the SetupScreen feedback loop or inject a digest failure.
- Trigger: Leave a recognized game-data pathname visible in the active internal or removable set while every open or read fails persistently, or place a directory under a recognized game filename so `findStaleFiles` admits it but `FileInputStream` rejects it
- Impact: The launcher can remain indefinitely in rapid hashing, logging, and recomposition work, repeatedly consuming storage IO, CPU, and battery while the launch controls oscillate or remain disabled. On fast failures the loop can become a tight resource storm; on slow failing storage it repeatedly queues expensive attempts and prevents the user from reaching a stable recovery state.
- Expected: One refresh generation attempts each stale identity at most once, records a typed terminal or retryable failure, and never changes its own effect key solely because an item failed. Retries are user-driven or use a bounded delayed policy that is canceled when the set, file identity, or Activity generation changes.
- Suggested fix: Return per-file typed hash outcomes and increment refresh only when pruning or a successful upsert actually changes projected state. Keep failed identities in an immutable error snapshot keyed by canonical path, length, modification identity, and active-set generation; display a retry or remove action, and apply bounded exponential backoff only for explicitly transient errors. Require `isFile` before hashing, suppress duplicate in-flight work, and clear failure state only when the file identity changes or the user requests retry.
- Validation: Drive the real effect with successful files plus absent, directory, permission-denied, immediate EIO, slow EIO, mid-read removal, and repeatedly changing files on internal and removable roots. Count digest calls, refresh-key changes, logs, recompositions, IO jobs, and launch-state transitions under virtual time and Activity/set replacement. Require one attempt per identity and generation, no tight loop or stale job, stable actionable error UI, cancellation on owner change, bounded explicit retries, and exact manifest publication after a later successful retry.

A larger unrelated, corrupt, or older nested file can displace the intended root identity, and identical on-disk input can select a different GOG source across devices or directory generations.

Treat explicit per-axis fields as current fractions, interpret the legacy single field according to the layout version that produced it, and update maintained presets to the current explicit per-axis schema. ### BR-0531: P2 - Validate ETC2 image dimensions with checked arithmetic

- [ ] OPEN
- Type: defect
- Confidence: high
- Category: correctness/memory-safety
- Found by: R1-CHUNK-0472
- Location: `c01d8fe4686c63d931b1e543a6305bbafaa944a9:android/tools/etc2tool/etc2tool.cpp:L36-L42,L47-L80,L107-L135,L154-L176,L202-L229` in power-of-two sizing, allocation, indexing, and mip construction
- Related: `android/tools/etc2tool/CMakeLists.txt:L36-L64`, pinned `stb_image.h:L198-L209,L795-L797,L1022-L1058,L5105-L5127`, `game_data/mods/d2x-xl/convert_d2xxl_textures.ps1`, and BR-0321
- Evidence: The tool accepts every image that `stbi_load` decodes, rounds width and height independently to powers of two, and performs `tw * th * 4`, `w * h`, `npix * 4`, downsample byte counts, and source and destination index products in signed `int` without a dimension or pixel budget. The pinned stb_image revision allows each dimension through 2^24 and decoded images below roughly 1 GiB. A one-channel PNG declaring 32,769 by 8,193 pixels has 268,476,417 decoded bytes, below stb_image's 2^30-pixel/byte check, but rounds to 65,536 by 16,384; the required RGBA allocation is exactly 4,294,967,296 bytes. Evaluating `calloc(tw * th * 4, 1)` therefore invokes signed-overflow undefined behavior and commonly passes zero. Since a zero-size allocation may return non-null, the function can then execute overflowing indices and write far outside that allocation. Smaller rounded products can request multi-gigabyte work with no tool-specific limit, and a failed later `downsample_rgba` allocation is assigned to `cur` without a null check before the next compression dereference. The maintained pack scripts happen to feed 256- or 512-pixel textures, but the documented standalone CLI accepts arbitrary PNG, JPEG, TGA, and BMP paths.
- Trigger: Run `etc2tool` on a compact grayscale PNG whose declared dimensions are 32,769 by 8,193, or another decoder-valid extreme-aspect image whose independently rounded RGBA product reaches or exceeds the signed or 32-bit allocation boundary; on a zero-returning allocation path, allow conversion to enter padding. Separately, fault a nonfinal mip downsample allocation.
- Impact: A malformed or merely oversized source can terminate the offline pack build, invoke undefined behavior, or corrupt heap memory instead of producing a bounded diagnostic failure. Automated conversion can lose the current item and continue building an incomplete texture archive, while a standalone invocation may damage its process state or machine stability through excessive allocation and CPU work.
- Expected: The tool validates source and rounded dimensions against an explicit texture and memory budget, computes every pixel, byte, index, mip, and codec size with checked unsigned arithmetic, and treats every intermediate allocation failure as a clean nonzero conversion failure before dereference or output publication.
- Suggested fix: Define a maximum dimension and aggregate pixel/working-set budget appropriate to the renderer or documented offline use. Before allocation, checked-multiply rounded width, height, four-byte RGBA storage, sixteen-byte float storage, ETC2 block storage, and cumulative mip storage in `size_t`, rejecting any value not representable by downstream `int` or `unsigned int` APIs. Use `size_t` for indices, check `downsample_rgba` before releasing the current level or advancing state, catch `std::bad_alloc`, and validate original dimensions against the metadata representation.
- Validation: Add grayscale, grayscale-alpha, RGB, and RGBA fixtures at ordinary dimensions, each exact configured boundary and boundary plus one, extreme aspect ratios, 32,769 by 8,193, dimensions around every power-of-two transition, and checked-product limits. Inject failure into padding, float conversion, mip-array, downsample, codec, KTX storage, metadata, and write allocations; run ASan and UBSan and require bounded nonzero failure, no zero-size success, no invalid access or signed overflow, no partial output, and unchanged ordinary pack hashes or documented replacements.

- Suggested fix: Acquire one OS-enforced exclusive resource atomically, such as a `FileStream` created with `CreateNew` and retained with no sharing for the complete run, or an atomic lock-directory creation with verified owner metadata. Update stage diagnostics through the held owner or a separate atomically replaced status file; never relinquish exclusivity while rewriting metadata.
- Validation: Synchronize two and then many process launches at an empty-lock barrier and at every stage transition; require exactly one owner, zero helper invocations from losers, no partial-marker stale classification, and cleanup after normal exit and exceptions. Retain a dead-owner recovery test that cannot remove a live owner's resource.

- Evidence: Each previously unseen client address, and each client/destination pair in symmetric modes, creates a new nonblocking UDP socket that is inserted into `mappings` and `reverse_map`. No timestamp, idle expiry, size limit, eviction, close, or shutdown cleanup ever removes one. Every loop copies all accumulated sockets into a `select.select` input list. The compose short-form port declarations publish all four client listeners on every host interface by default, so repeated ordinary source-port changes or a reachable sender spraying datagrams from fresh UDP source ports can grow descriptors without bound. Once a socket descriptor exceeds the platform `select` set limit, `select.select` raises `ValueError`; the handler merely continues with the same oversized permanent mapping set, producing a tight loop that can neither receive traffic nor recover.
- Trigger: Keep a container alive across enough client socket rotations, or send UDP datagrams to any published proxy port from enough distinct source endpoints to push its external sockets beyond the process or `select` descriptor limit.

Because setup's reachability probe only verifies that UDP send returns, it can still label the broken ports reachable.
- Expected: NAT mappings have a bounded lifecycle and descriptor count, inactive mappings release their sockets and reverse state, externally reachable listeners cannot be used to allocate unlimited testbed resources, and polling failures either recover by removing invalid state or terminate visibly.
- Suggested fix: Track last activity per mapping, expire and close idle sockets, impose a conservative global and per-client mapping cap, and remove every associated reverse entry atomically. Use `selectors`/poll for the supported descriptor range, but still enforce budgets; do not swallow an unchanged descriptor-limit failure. Bind published host ports to the narrow interface needed by the emulators or firewall the testbed, and make setup verify an actual valid round trip plus container health.
- Validation: Reuse and rotate client source ports across every NAT type, exceed each configured mapping budget, wait through expiry, and assert descriptor and mapping counts return to baseline and old ports can be rebound. Drive the descriptor-limit path and require bounded CPU plus explicit health failure or recovery. ### BR-0579: P2 - Commit dependency configuration changes as one atomic generation

- [ ] OPEN
- Type: defect
- Confidence: high
- Category: build-release/transactionality
- Found by: R1-CHUNK-0489
- Location: `c01d8fe4686c63d931b1e543a6305bbafaa944a9:android/get_deps/check-updates.ps1:L1627-L1644,L1670-L1798`
- Related: `android/get_deps/tool_versions.conf`; `android/gradle/wrapper/gradle-wrapper.properties`; BR-0563; BR-0577
- Evidence: `Update-Conf` rereads and directly truncates the public manifest for every single key. One dependency selection can invoke it repeatedly: NDK publishes short version, URL, and independently derived full version; JDK publishes version, major, and URL; Chromaprint and decoder updates publish commit/version plus multiple URLs and directory names; soundfont publishes version and URL; Gradle separately rewrites wrapper properties. There is no lock, staging file, flush, atomic replace, rollback, or cross-file generation marker. Interruption or an exception between calls leaves a mixed identity, interruption during `Set-Content` can truncate the only manifest, and concurrent updater processes can overwrite each other's read-modify-write results. Installers may run against that intermediate public state before the selected batch finishes.
- Trigger: Interrupt or fail a multi-key target after any individual write, lose power during `Set-Content`, run two target selections concurrently, or fail an immediate install-sync after its target fields have already changed.
- Impact: Every Gradle build and dependency helper can consume a truncated or internally inconsistent manifest, select URLs and directories for different releases, or pair Gradle properties with a different target. A failed maintenance run can destroy the previously working configuration and requires manual reconstruction.
- Expected: All validated fields and related wrapper metadata for the selected dependency set appear as one complete durable generation, while any failure or competing invocation preserves the prior valid generation.
- Suggested fix: Acquire one update lock, build and validate a complete typed manifest and related-file plan in memory, write unique sibling files, flush them, and atomically replace only after all semantic, digest, compatibility, and installer preconditions pass. For multiple files, use a recoverable transaction marker or stage a generated configuration directory and switch one pointer; restore the prior generation on failure.
- Validation: Inject failure, access denial, and process termination before, during, and after every field and wrapper write; run barrier-synchronized updaters with disjoint and overlapping selections; and fail immediate installers. At every boundary require either the byte-identical prior generation or one complete validated new generation, never truncation, lost updates, mixed identities, or consumers observing intermediate state.
- Resolution: Pending

### BR-0580: P2 - Derive both NDK version forms from one release record

- [ ] OPEN
- Type: defect
- Confidence: high
- Category: build-release/correctness
- Found by: R1-CHUNK-0489
- Location: `c01d8fe4686c63d931b1e543a6305bbafaa944a9:android/get_deps/check-updates.ps1:L988-L999,L1075-L1077,L1172-L1173,L1220-L1224,L1688-L1697`
- Related: `android/get_deps/tool_versions.conf:L16-L19`; `android/get_deps/helpers/get_ndk.sh:L11-L43`; `android/app/build.gradle:L276-L277`
- Evidence: The updater scrapes the first `rNNx` archive name from the human download page for `NDK_VERSION`, but independently takes the numerically greatest `ndk;<numeric>` path from the complete SDK repository for `NDK_FULL_VERSION`; it does not correlate the two records or inspect repository channel metadata. It then publishes both as if they identify one release. The installer downloads and names its directory from the short tag, while Gradle declares the independent numeric version and points `ndkPath` at that directory. If the page order differs from the repository maximum or the repository contains a higher preview channel, a normal update installs one NDK and tells Gradle to require another.
- Trigger: Let the download page's first stable/LTS archive and the greatest numeric SDK-repository package differ because of page ordering, staggered publication, beta/canary channels, or transient metadata snapshots, then select the Android NDK target.
- Impact: Clean setup can successfully download the short-tag NDK but Gradle rejects its `source.properties` version against `android.ndkVersion`, or resolves a different SDK-managed NDK; native builds then fail or vary by host inventory while the manifest appears fully updated.
- Expected: Short tag, full revision, channel, per-platform archive URL, extracted source metadata, and Gradle declaration all come from and validate one exact release record.
- Suggested fix: Resolve a structured NDK release catalog keyed by one stable channel entry, map its short and full identities explicitly, and verify downloaded `source.properties` before publication. Never combine independent maxima; if no authoritative mapping is available, retain the prior target and require reviewed manual pairing.
- Validation: Test stable, LTS, beta, canary, staggered, reordered-page, missing-platform, and inconsistent metadata fixtures. Require the updater to choose one permitted record or decline, the installer directory's `Pkg.Revision` to equal `NDK_FULL_VERSION`, and Gradle to use that same path on every supported host.
- Resolution: Pending

### BR-0581: P1 - Reject remote version text that can execute when the manifest is sourced

- [ ] OPEN
- Type: defect
- Confidence: high
- Category: security/supply-chain
- Found by: R1-CHUNK-0489
- Location: `c01d8fe4686c63d931b1e543a6305bbafaa944a9:android/get_deps/check-updates.ps1:L921-L950,L1151-L1156,L1178-L1380,L1458-L1473,L1627-L1636,L1670-L1789`
- Related: `android/get_deps/tool_versions.conf`; every Bash helper that uses `source "$SCRIPT_DIR/../tool_versions.conf"`; `android/get_deps/get_all.sh:L17-L19`; BR-0157
- Evidence: Latest values originate in remote Git tags, Maven/PyPI metadata, redirects, and scraped pages. The version parser extracts digits for ordering but returns the complete original string, and `Update-Conf` writes it unquoted and unescaped into a file deliberately sourced as Bash code. Git permits tag text containing `$` and parentheses: a focused `git check-ref-format 'refs/tags/v999$(Write-Output_PWNED)'` succeeded, and the updater normalizer retained `999$(Write-Output_PWNED)` as numeric version 999. A harmless Bash probe sourcing the equivalent assignment performs command substitution. Thus compromise of any queried tag namespace—or accepted hostile metadata with shell metacharacters—can turn a user selecting the visible update, especially `all`, into command execution as soon as immediate install-sync or any later dependency helper sources the manifest, before artifact digest validation can protect downloads.
- Trigger: A queried upstream publishes or an attacker with tag/repository control injects a numerically newer tag such as `v999$(attacker_command)`, then a maintainer selects that row or all target updates and reaches any Bash dependency helper.
- Impact: Remote metadata can execute arbitrary commands with the developer or CI account's permissions, modify the repository and dependency cache, steal credentials, or subvert subsequent builds. Manual version selection is not a safe code-review boundary because the table treats the string as a version and never identifies it as executable shell syntax.
- Expected: Remote discovery data remains inert typed data through comparison, display, persistence, and consumption; only a narrow canonical version/commit grammar can enter the manifest, and sourcing configuration never executes stored values.
- Suggested fix: Stop using an executable shell file as the shared data format; store versions and URLs in strict JSON/TOML or another parser-only format and pass values as data. Until migration, allowlist an exact grammar per key, reject every metacharacter or control character before display and write, quote with a proven shell serializer, validate commit fields as exact hex, and require reviewed authenticated metadata plus BR-0157 digests.
- Validation: Feed Git, Maven, PyPI, redirect, and page fixtures containing `$()`, backticks, parameter expansion, separators, quotes, whitespace, newlines/entities, glob syntax, option prefixes, Unicode controls, huge components, and ordinary valid versions. Require rejection before selection or file mutation, byte-identical prior configuration, no command or network side effect when every helper reads accepted configuration, and normal updates for the complete allowlisted corpus.
- Resolution: Pending

- Evidence: Both frozen scan functions invoke the D1 or D2 headless executable synchronously with PowerShell's call operator and return only after the child exits. They provide no wall-clock deadline, cancellation route, process-tree termination, or partial-log recovery. A malformed mission can already drive the BR-0468 arithmetic loop indefinitely, and any other engine, filesystem, or toolchain stall has the same ownership outcome: the per-archive `try/catch` is never regained, no failure record or final summary is written, later archives do not run, and the outer device wrapper cannot supervise this separate host path. Live commit `b16e7737` replaced these exact calls with a process wrapper whose default timeout is 120 seconds and kills the child tree, independently confirming the missing frozen lifecycle boundary.
- Trigger: Regenerate an archive whose headless scanner loops or blocks, including BR-0468's extreme-coordinate mission, or use a child fixture that starts successfully and never exits; the built-in Counterstrike path has the same behavior before archive iteration starts.
- Impact: One input can hang the complete interactive or unattended regression regeneration indefinitely, retain its engine process and files, suppress every later result and final status, and require killing the parent process without a trustworthy summary of which checked-in outputs were changed.
- Expected: Every headless scan has a documented finite wall-clock budget, continuously drains diagnostics, terminates the complete owned process tree on timeout or cancellation, records a precise per-source failure, and either continues or aborts under an explicit batch policy.
- Suggested fix: Use the bounded asynchronous process wrapper added after the frozen head (or a shared equivalent), make the deadline configurable with a safe finite default, kill and wait for the complete child tree in `finally`, preserve stdout and stderr, and apply it to both archive and built-in scans. Keep BR-0468's native arithmetic correction because a wrapper timeout contains rather than repairs that defect.
- Validation: Run ordinary D1 and D2 scans plus fixtures that exit nonzero, hang before output, hang after partial stdout/stderr, spawn a descendant, ignore graceful termination, and trigger BR-0468. Require completion within the configured bound, no surviving child or descendant, truthful logs and status, later-item behavior matching policy, and unchanged successful metadata output.
